holdReason: Insufficient individually-attributable behavioural evidence (attribution not confirmed after reading). The historical individual is documented almost entirely through the poems themselves: every source read says that most biographical detail comes from the poems, that her parentage, marriage, concubinage and even birth and death years are disputed (proposed dates range from 1735 to 1869), and that some critics argue she never existed and that the verse was written by lesser poets or failed scholars. The main documentary anchor, the Luu Huong Ky manuscript found in 1964 with an 1814 foreword by Ton Phong Thi, is itself questioned for its style and transmission, and the famous double-entendre poems survive through oral tradition and woodblock editions from 1893 on, with estimates of her output ranging from 46 to 213 poems. No dated act, decision or attributable episode can be tied to a historical person, so any trait row would be inferred from a disputed corpus or from legend, which the pre-modern rules forbid. Identity and the significance research are kept; the profile is held at zero rows pending a lead decision, as with Laozi in Roster63.

sources.title: Hồ Xuân Hương (Q465259), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-05): label 'Hồ Xuân Hương', description 'The World Cultural Celebrity of Viet Nam', born 1772 and died 1822 (year precision only), citizen of Vietnam, occupations poet and writer, Korean label 호쑤언흐엉. Orientation only; not used as support for any claim.

Academy of American Poets (Poets.org), 'Hồ Xuân Hương' poet biography (page read in full, about 600 words). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Vietnamese poet of the late Lê dynasty called the 'Queen of Nôm poetry', who wrote mainly in the Nôm script in the Tang-style regulated verse form with double entendres mixing erotic imagery and everyday objects, critiquing social hypocrisy and the treatment of women; says biographical details vary and come largely from the poems, that some scholars hold she may not have existed (a persona invented by a group of scholars), that her output is debated at 46 to 213 poems, that the earliest surviving hand-copied volume was commissioned in 1893, and names her main modern translators and scholars (Durand 1968, Balaban 2000).

Thúy Đinh, 'Hồ Xuân Hương, Poet of Nimble Essence', American Poets magazine (Academy of American Poets), essay of 22 May 2026 (read in full). Personal and interpretive essay by a translator: cites the 1964 Lưu Hương Ký manuscript (24 Classical Chinese and 28 Nôm poems, foreword dated 1814 by Tốn Phong Thị) as the main documentary evidence, notes that many Vietnamese critics do not regard it as representative, that the famous poems survive through oral tradition and woodblock editions of 1893 to 1922, that proposed life dates range from 1735 to 1869, and that some critics argue she never existed. Critical and uncertainty voice on the evidence.

John Balaban, 'Hồ Xuân Hương Introduction', Vietnamese Nôm Preservation Foundation, Nôm Project (page read in full, about 1,500 words). Translator's introduction: little is firmly documented, most biographical detail comes from the poems, her family origins and status as a concubine are disputed, some readers doubt she existed and others think part of the corpus is by anonymous writers, estimates of her output range from about 25 to 148 poems; describes her Nôm regulated-verse poems with tonal-pun double meanings and the themes of male authority, marriage rules, concubinage, love and corrupt clergy. A translator and admirer, so reception evidence is admiring.

John Balaban, 'Ho Xuan Huong: Poetry', Tricycle: The Buddhist Review (only the free introduction was readable; the poems, commentary and fuller discussion are behind a paywall and were not opened). States that she was born around 1780, was a high-ranking concubine, wrote in Nôm using Chinese classical forms, satirised the decaying Buddhist church and Confucian male society, and that her poems were copied by hand for nearly a century before a 1909 woodblock printing. Partly read only.
